parsed.explanation: The quote is faithful. The text establishes only that V contains at most one positive value; from f(x)>0 it notes merely g(x)>-x, and nowhere in §1–§7 does it prove g(x)≥0. The standard one-line argument — if g(u)<0 then f^n(u)=u+n g(u)>0 for all n, impossible for large n — is absent. Hence 'Consequently, either (i) g≡0 or (ii) V⊆{0,c}' omits the a priori possible case that g attains negative values (possibly together with 0 and/or one positive value), and the entire §4–§6 analysis, which presupposes V⊆{0,c}, never addresses it. Also, §3's progression argument explicitly assumes c1,c2>0, confirming negative values are never handled. The witness's diagnosis and repair are correct; as written the necessity case analysis is incomplete, though fixable by the orbit-positivity argument.
